newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore opposition attacks electoral changes.
newsitem.headline: Singapore opposition attacks electoral changes.

text.p: Singapore opposition parties have attacked proposed electoral changes as weakening their chances of winning, the Straits Times said on Wednesday.

It quoted Singapore Democratic Party (SDP) assistant secretary-general Kwan Yue Keng as calling the changes "a series of measures released close to election time, designed to further entrench PAP (People's Action Party) rule."

Bills introduced in parliament on Tuesday by Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong would raise the maximum number of members of parliament (MPs) who can be elected from a multi-member constituency from four to six.
In these constituencies, votes are cast for slates rather than individual candidates. The slate that wins the most votes takes all of the seats in the constituency.
Of 81 elected seats in parliament, the opposition currently holds just four, all from single-seat constituencies.
The proposed changes would also permit a reduction of single-member constituencies from the current 21 to as few as eight.
That could mean more three-cornered fights in the remaining single-seat wards, splitting the opposition and hurting its chances, opposition leaders were quoted as saying.
"Three-cornered fights would definitely occur, and the opposition votes would suffer," said Singapore People's Party leader Sin Kek Tong.
In multi-seat constituencies, heavyweight PAP ministers could "provide an umbrella for new and possibly weak candidates," said National Solidarity Party head Tan Chee Kien.
PAP members said the proposed changes would allow for better management of town councils under the care of a group of MPs.

MP R. Sinnakaruppan said larger, multi-member constituencies would give Goh flexibility to implement his vision of having community development councils oversee other grassroots bodies and promote community-bonding.
PAP MPs also said the opposition could win big if it captured a multi-member constituency.
MP Koh Lip Lin dismissed claims of PAP bullying, saying: "The government always has the advantage; it is not a question of fair or unfair."
The bills are due for parliamentary debate at a later date.
Singapore must hold a general election by April 1997.
